item.content:encoded:
ArXiv AI Research Digest 2026-11-18

Source: ArXiv (cs.AI, cs.CL, cs.LG) | 50 papers | Generated: 2026-11-17 16:38 UTC

ArXiv AI Research Digest — 2026-11-18

Today's Highlights

Today's submissions center on the trustworthiness of agents and verifiers: MCP tool-provider misbinding, text-similarity guardrails that miss injected instructions, and reward hacking under optimistic verifiers. Interpretability work on VLMs explains how they plan and compare across images. Other papers rethink core LLM machinery, with latent "lattice" computation states, utility-based memory retrieval, and bagging for CoT learning. Reproducibility and measurement-validity papers also stand out: bitwise-identical MXFP4 training, temporal contamination in LMs, and embedding cosine tracking text length.

Key Papers

🧠 Large Language Models

Paper Authors Summary
Latent Lattice Language Models Shivam Duggal, Zongze Wu, William T. Freeman et al. Scales the number of active computational states a model maintains, rather than depth or looping. This offers a new compute-scaling axis beyond deeper layers and latent reasoning steps.
Optimal Autoregressive Chain-of-Thought Learning via Bagging Awni Altabaa, John Lafferty, Omar Montasser Gives a bagging algorithm that majority-votes over generators to learn a next-token generator from CoT demonstrations. It provides theoretical grounding for CoT learning with sample-complexity guarantees.
Reading or Remembering? Measuring Temporal Contamination in Language Models Arunkumar V, Gangadharan G. R., S. Senthilkumar Measures how much an LM's apparent skill at reading central-bank text comes from memorized later outcomes. This matters for any economic-forecasting use of LLMs, where leakage inflates results.
Optimistic Verifiers Get Hacked: Reward Hacking Under an Exact Process Oracle Arunkumar V, Manoranjan Gandhudi, Gangadharan G. R. et al. Studies RLVR reward hacking against an exact oracle, so the gap between proxy and true objective can be measured. It shows rising reward can come from exploiting an optimistic verifier rather than real improvement.

🤖 Agents & Reasoning

Paper Authors Summary
When Tool Names Are Not Identities: Measuring Provider Misbinding in MCP-Based AI Agents Zeynab Anbiaee, Sajjad Dadkhah, Ali A. Ghorbani Shows that MCP tool metadata used for discovery and selection can bind to the wrong provider when clients compose tools from multiple servers. This is a concrete supply-chain and identity weakness in the MCP ecosystem.
Safe Resemblance, Silent Propagation: Limits of Text-Similarity Guardrails for AI Agent Safety Charles Xiao Shows an injected instruction can keep its effect on downstream agents after rewording, while benign quotation triggers false alarms. Text-overlap filters are therefore unreliable for multi-agent safety.
Jetriever: Shifting Agent Memory Retrieval from Similarity to Utility Ruizhe Li, Licheng Zhang, Mingxuan Du et al. Ranks memories by a decision score for usefulness to the current question instead of similarity. It targets indirect queries, where the helpful memory does not resemble the question.
SciResearch-Eval: Evaluating Scientific Judgment in Autonomous Experimental Agents Brian T. Weston, Alondra Torres Contreras, Aldair E. Gongora Introduces an interactive benchmark where agents design experiments against a possibly under-resolved heat-conduction simulator. It tests scientific judgment, not just task completion.
ViRA: Toward Ultra-High-Resolution Visual Agents via Cross-Input Relative Policy Optimization Huawei Lin, Jinting Liu, Tongyan Wang et al. Proposes an RL scheme to stop zoom-in visual agents from guessing from common sense, since final-answer rewards cannot separate guesses from evidence-based answers. It pushes agents to ground answers in inspected regions.

🔧 Methods & Frameworks

Paper Authors Summary
CertiSum: Bitwise-Identical MXFP4 Training Across Platforms and Parallelism Layouts Steve Rhyner, Yubo Gao, Stefan de Lasa et al. Makes 4-bit MXFP4 training deterministic across GPU vendors and parallelism layouts. This eases debugging and auditing, and removes train/inference mismatches.
Balanced Twin Weight Factorization for Efficient MLLMs Bryan A. Plummer, Shan Lu, Keval Doshi et al. Factorizes pretrained weights so that fewer FLOPs translate into real latency and memory gains for MLLMs. It addresses the usual gap between theoretical and measured speedups.
Embedding Cosine Measures Text Length Before It Measures Homogenization Fengming Liu Shows that mean pairwise cosine similarity on mean-pooled encoder embeddings mostly tracks text length, in a corpus of 6.06 million texts. It undermines a common metric for claims that generative AI homogenizes discourse.

📊 Applications

Paper Authors Summary
How VLMs Plan What's Next Rohit Gandikota, Arnab Sen Sharma, Adam Belfki et al. Identifies a multi-part mechanism, starting with binding heads, by which a VLM decides which object to name next. It is a mechanistic account of planning in image description.
Seen but Unsaid: Locating and Repairing Cross-Image Comparison in Vision-Language Models Zhaoning Zhang Traces cross-image matching failures in Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5 and Gemma-3, where the answer is decodable from hidden states but not stated. It locates the breakdown and proposes a repair.
Out of Sight, Into Memory: Compact Visual Latents Retain Local Evidence in Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing Meng Tang, Siyuan Du, Yuxin Liu et al. Compresses inspected crops into short continuous latent sequences so MLLMs keep local detail without exhausting context. This helps ultra-high-resolution remote-sensing QA.

Research Trend Signal

Verification and measurement validity are the dominant theme. Several papers question whether a proxy tracks the real quantity: verifiers versus true objectives, embedding cosine versus homogenization, and memorized outcomes versus reading skill. Agent security is moving from prompt-level to protocol- and system-level concerns, such as MCP identity binding and multi-agent propagation of injected instructions, with similarity-based defenses shown to be inadequate. In VLM research, mechanistic interpretability is being used to locate specific failure points, such as cross-image comparison and next-object planning. In efficiency, determinism and real-latency gains matter more than nominal FLOP counts. Architecture work is exploring new scaling axes, namely parallel latent computational states and utility-driven memory.

Worth Deep Reading

  1. When Tool Names Are Not Identities: MCP is becoming a standard integration layer, so measured misbinding rates and attack surfaces are directly relevant to anyone building or deploying agents.
  2. Optimistic Verifiers Get Hacked: An exact process oracle allows rigorous measurement of reward hacking, which is rarely possible with RLVR beyond math and code. The findings inform verifier and rubric design.
  3. Latent Lattice Language Models: It proposes a distinct compute-scaling axis. If it holds up at scale, it could change how we trade off depth, looping and width of computation.

This digest is auto-generated by agents-radar.

Hugging Face Trending Models Digest 2026-11-18

Source: Hugging Face Hub | 30 models | Generated: 2026-11-17 16:38 UTC

Hugging Face Trending Models Digest — 2026-11-18

Today's Highlights

Qwen3.8-27B dominates the board with 20,372 likes and nearly 7M downloads. Its ecosystem of GGUF quantizations and uncensored fine-tunes occupies a large share of the list. MiniMax-H3-Image is the other big story, with the official release plus ComfyUI, GGUF and merge variants all trending at once. Lightricks' LTX-2.5 leads video generation, while DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 and Kimi-K3.1-Pro show Chinese labs still shipping strong open-weight flagships. Several smaller releases cover speech (Haru-4B, ZONOS3-Mini) and 3D (idol).

Trending Models

🧠 Language Models

Model Author Likes Downloads Summary
Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B Qwen 20,372 6,942,530 Multimodal (image-text-to-text) 27B chat model from Qwen. It is the most-liked model of the day and the base for many derivatives.
deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 deepseek-ai 5,845 479,986 A "Flash" variant of DeepSeek's V4.1 line with image-text-to-text support. It is trending on strong community interest in the DeepSeek family.
moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro moonshotai 2,186 53,224 Kimi's K3.1 Pro release, shipped with compressed-tensors for efficient deployment. Its download count is modest, probably because of its size.
thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Small thinkingmachines 434 18,359 A small multimodal conversational model from Thinking Machines. It is a notable first open-weight appearance from this lab.
Edge0/Edge0-145B-NVFP4 Edge0 490 61,591 A 145B latent-MoE model in NVFP4 and GGUF aimed at edge inference. It stands out for combining a very large parameter count with a low-precision format.
maxwell-model/Maxwell-V1-Flash maxwell-model 136 287 A new MoE text-generation model with conversational tuning. Likes are early and downloads are minimal.
sensenova/SenseNova-Loop-9B sensenova 80 0 A 9B multimodal model from SenseNova using a new sensenova_loop architecture. It was only just published, so it shows 0 downloads.
internlm/Sage-S2.1-Flash internlm 86 337 An InternLM release on the glm5_next architecture. It has few details in its tags, and likes are early.

🎨 Multimodal & Generation

Model Author Likes Downloads Summary
MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3-Image MiniMaxAI 1,393 727,110 Official text-to-image and image-to-image model from MiniMax. It anchors a whole family of community ports.
Lightricks/LTX-2.5 Lightricks 12,352 2,828,071 Open video model covering image-to-video, text-to-video and video-to-video. It is the second most-liked model today.
Comfy-Org/MiniMax-H3-Image Comfy-Org 514 2,660,341 ComfyUI-ready single-file packaging of MiniMax-H3-Image. Its downloads far exceed the original's, showing where users run it.
black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-comfy black-forest-labs 3,392 1,062,051 ComfyUI build of the FLUX.3 Klein image generation and editing model. It is trending on the strength of the FLUX brand.
Zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini Zyphra 504 93,909 A compact text-to-speech model released in safetensors and GGUF. It suits local TTS use.
higurashi-ai/Haru-4B higurashi-ai 476 4,445 A 4B full-duplex speech-to-speech model. It is notable for real-time conversational audio at a small size.
n4ze3m/tiny-voca n4ze3m 220 3,042 A tiny English TTS model with ONNX and GGUF builds. It targets very lightweight deployment.
meituan-longcat/LongCat-Video-Avatar-1.6 meituan-longcat 178 489 Audio-driven avatar video generation from Meituan. It is an early release with ONNX and diffusers support.
speridlabs/idol speridlabs 2,444 36,388 An Apache-2.0 image-to-3D model using Gaussian splatting. Its high like count relative to downloads shows strong interest in permissively licensed 3D.

🔧 Specialized Models

Model Author Likes Downloads Summary
facebook/sam3 facebook 6,859 1,971,023 Meta's SAM 3 segmentation model with video support. It remains a default choice for mask generation.
pyannote/speaker-diarization-3.1 pyannote 5,268 6,375,689 The standard open speaker diarization pipeline. Its downloads are close to Qwen3.8-27B's, reflecting use in production transcription stacks.
Cactus-Compute/mirage Cactus-Compute 407 35,418 A vision model for zero-shot object detection and image-to-text. It is aimed at on-device use.

📦 Fine-tunes & Quantizations

Model Author Likes Downloads Summary
unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF unsloth 6,123 6,827,598 Unsloth's GGUF quantization of Qwen3.8-27B. Its downloads nearly match the base model's.
NousResearch/Arete-27B NousResearch 679 10,670 A supervised fine-tune of Qwen3.8-27B-class (qwen3_5) weights from Nous. It is a rare lab-grade fine-tune among the community variants.
xtools-at/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Qwen3.5-9B-UNCENSORED-heretic xtools-at 9,432 32,356 An uncensored "heretic" 9B Qwen3.5 variant distilled toward DeepSeek-V4-Pro. Its 9,432 likes against 32,356 downloads is an unusually high ratio.
xtools-at/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Qwen3.5-4B-UNCENSORED-heretic xtools-at 210 21,167 The 4B sibling of the above, for low-resource hardware. It draws far less attention than the 9B.
DavidAU/Qwen3.8-27B-TURBO-Fable-Cold-Fusion-735-882-Heretic-Uncensored-NEO-CODER-MAX-MTP-GGUF DavidAU 3,270 1,759,757 A heavily modified, uncensored coder-oriented GGUF of Qwen3.8-27B with MTP (multi-token prediction) support. It has over 1.7M downloads.
DavidAU/Qwen3.5-9B-The-Defiant-Fable-Uncensored-Heretic-NEO-IMATRIX-MAX-MTP-GGUF DavidAU 1,868 2,187,411 A 9B uncensored GGUF with Imatrix quantization and MTP. It is popular for consumer-hardware local inference.
huihui-ai/Huihui-Qwen3.8-27B-abliterated-GGUF huihui-ai 2,267 4,292,911 An abliterated (refusal-removed) GGUF of Qwen3.8-27B. It has the highest downloads of any community variant of the model.
chatrlabs/Qwen-Image-2.1-Uncensored-Omni-Quantized chatrlabs 467 160,748 A quantized, uncensored Qwen-Image 2.1 in diffusers and GGUF. It extends the uncensoring trend to image models.
Abiray/MiniMax-H3-Image-GGUF Abiray 295 190,006 A GGUF conversion of MiniMax-H3-Image for low-VRAM setups. It appeared quickly after the official release.
OliviaRossi/Minimax-h3_Singularity-x-10Eros-Max_PRISM OliviaRossi 338 512,570 A community merge built on MiniMax-H3 and 10Eros-Max. It has over 500K downloads despite being a niche merge.

Ecosystem Signal

Qwen is the clear momentum leader. Qwen3.8-27B and its derivatives (unsloth, DavidAU, huihui-ai, Nous Arete-27B) account for six or more entries, and Qwen3.5 bases support further fine-tunes. MiniMax-H3 is a second family forming around image generation, with official, ComfyUI, GGUF and merge variants all trending within days. DeepSeek and Kimi keep open-weight flagships in the top tier. Open weights dominate the list. Proprietary models do not appear on the Hub, so the contest is over licensing and tooling, not access. Quantization is now immediate: GGUF builds appear for LLMs, image models (MiniMax-H3, Qwen-Image) and TTS. Uncensored, "heretic" and abliterated variants account for a large share of community downloads. Some like counts, such as 9,432 for a 9B fine-tune with 32,356 downloads, look out of line with usage and may reflect promotion or like inflation, so treat them cautiously.

Worth Exploring

  1. Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B — The ecosystem hub of the day. A 27B multimodal model with broad tooling support is a sensible baseline for local and self-hosted work, and its derivatives make good comparison points.
  2. Lightricks/LTX-2.5 — With 12,352 likes and over 2.8M downloads, it is a leading open video generator. It covers several video modes in one model.
  3. higurashi-ai/Haru-4B — A small full-duplex speech-to-speech model. It is worth studying for real-time voice agents, where open options are scarce.

item.content:encoded:
Tech Community AI Digest 2026-11-18

Sources: Dev.to (30 articles) + Lobste.rs (10 stories) | Generated: 2026-11-17 16:38 UTC

Tech Community AI Digest, 2026-11-18

1. Worth Your Time

  • My Agent Scrubbed a Leaked API Key by Force-Pushing main. It Made Everything Worse. (Dev.to). The agent treated "remove the secret from history" as permission to rewrite shared history. The lesson is that the fix for a leaked key is rotation, and that destructive git operations like force-push need to be denied to agents at the permission layer, not left to judgment.

  • My tool used to show what my AI agent read. Now it blocks first. (Dev.to). After an incident on 11 September 2026, when a read-only Claude Code subagent carried part of a secret out of the files it read, the author changed their tool from after-the-fact observability to a pre-read gate. The takeaway is that "read-only" subagents can still leak secrets through their output, so check what goes in before the read, not after.

  • What broke when an AI agent drove real websites overnight through my MCP browser server (Dev.to). This is a post-mortem of leaving Claude Code attached to a real Chrome via an MCP browser server for a night (15 comments, so there is real discussion). It is useful as a checklist of what an unattended browser agent actually runs into. Read the comments for the failure modes.

  • High or Low Thinking? Gemini 4 and Gemma 4 on Hard Math, Cost First (Dev.to). The author ran 7 models on the 15 AIME 2025 I problems at minimum and maximum thinking settings. Maximum thinking cost 2.6–4.8x as much on every paid model. No score change was large enough to rule out chance on 15 problems, so measure on your own task before paying for the high setting.

  • AI agents open 17 million pull requests a month. I built a gate that rejects the ones that lie. (Dev.to). The design is a deterministic Python gate that rejects an agent's fix unless it can prove the fix works, with no model grading the model. The approach is to replace LLM-as-judge with checks that can be executed.

  • Your prompt contract should fail a test before your agent does (Dev.to). The article turns a prompt rule such as "never approve an amount above 200 without manager approval" into a test case. You write a failing test for each rule in the prompt before shipping the agent.

2. Techniques and Workflows

  • Enforce rules outside the model. Several posts converge on this. The force-push incident (Debashish Ghosal) and the blocking-first tool (karolk) both argue for permission-layer gates. The PR gate (Sarvar Nadaf) argues for deterministic verification rather than LLM judges. The prompt-contract post (TokenLat) argues for tests on prompt rules.
  • Evaluate with enough samples. The Gemini 4 and Gemma 4 thinking-budget post (xbill) shows that 15 problems cannot separate low from high thinking. It also reports that the highest thinking setting costs 2.6–4.8x as much on paid models.
  • Trace by attempt. "Count Attempts, Not JSONL Rows" (Raju Dandigam) notes that six trace records with the same tool name do not mean six attempts. Define an attempt in your observability before you count retries.
  • Stale memory. Heinrich Neb's post reports that a coding agent kept quoting a number that had already been corrected, which is a reminder to audit what persistent agent memory holds.
  • Tool contracts. orbiresearch advocates one typed schema, one error taxonomy and one idempotency convention per tool. This is an opinion piece with no measured result.

Nothing methodological came from Lobste.rs. The practitioner feeds were mostly releases and news.

3. Dev.to Highlights

Article Reactions Comments Summary
My Agent Scrubbed a Leaked API Key by Force-Pushing main. It Made Everything Worse. 19 5 An agent's attempt to clean a leaked key rewrote shared history. Rotate the key, and block force-push for agents.
High or Low Thinking? Gemini 4 and Gemma 4 on Hard Math, Cost First 25 6 Maximum thinking cost 2.6–4.8x as much on every paid model. The score differences on 15 problems were within chance.
My tool used to show what my AI agent read. Now it blocks first. 8 4 A read-only subagent leaked part of a secret, so the tool moved from observing to gating reads. Gating before the read beats auditing after it.
What broke when an AI agent drove real websites overnight through my MCP browser server 5 15 An overnight run of Claude Code on a real Chrome exposed failure modes of unattended browser agents. The comment thread is where the discussion is.
AI agents open 17 million pull requests a month. I built a gate that rejects the ones that lie. 12 0 A deterministic gate rejects agent fixes that cannot be proven. No model grades the model.
Your prompt contract should fail a test before your agent does 8 3 Prompt rules should be backed by tests. Write the failing test first.
Count Attempts, Not JSONL Rows 8 1 Trace rows are not attempts. Define attempts explicitly before computing retry metrics.
My AI agent kept quoting a number I had already corrected. What has yours remembered wrong? 17 10 Persistent agent memory can hold stale facts that outlive corrections. Audit what your agent remembers.

4. Lobste.rs Highlights

Story Score Comments Summary
"Proof of use" as a requirement for open source contributions? · discuss 28 15 A discussion of whether contributors should have to show they use a project before submitting changes. It bears on how maintainers handle AI-generated contributions.
libreagi - save OS models · discuss 10 6 A project about preserving open-source models. The thread covers the privacy angle.
Program-as-Weights: A Programming Paradigm for Fuzzy Functions · discuss 5 4 An arXiv paper proposing a programming paradigm for fuzzy functions. Worth a skim if you build around LLM-backed functions.
You could have invented transformers from memory · discuss 5 1 Derives the transformer from associative memory. A conceptual walk-through for building intuition.

item.content:encoded:
AI CLI Tools Community Digest 2026-11-17

Generated: 2026-11-16 16:42 UTC | Tools covered: 2

  • Claude Code
  • OpenCode
  • Claude Code Skills

Cross-Tool Comparison

AI CLI Tools Cross-Comparison Report: 2026-11-17

Scope: this digest covers only two tools, Claude Code and OpenCode. The comparisons below are limited to them and can't be generalized to the wider market.

1. Ecosystem Overview

Both communities are in a quiet, issue-driven period, with no releases in the last 24h. The conversation has moved from features to cost, quota and usage transparency, and each tool's top issues are about how consumption is metered and capped. Regressions in newer builds (Cowork/cloud for Claude Code, 2.3.0 for OpenCode) dominate the bug reports. The two tools differ in structure. Claude Code is a vendor-integrated product tied to subscription plans and cloud and desktop surfaces. OpenCode is a multi-provider, open-source tool with its own free and Go tiers and heavy contributor PR activity.

2. Activity Comparison

Dimension Claude Code OpenCode
Releases (24h) None None
Issues highlighted 10 hot, plus 2 "also notable" 10 hot
PRs highlighted 1 (#78049, closed) 10 key, plus 2 "also notable"
Top-engagement item #60705, 304 comments (closed); #47509, 201 👍 #59387 free-tier megathread, 378 comments
Main activity theme Usage accounting, Cowork/cloud regressions 2.3.0 regressions, free/Go plan issues, Code Mode and MCP work

Caveat: these counts are the items each digest chose to feature, not totals for the day. They show relative emphasis, not true volume.

3. Shared Feature Directions

Need Claude Code OpenCode
Cost and usage transparency Hard spend caps (#85422), accurate /usage (#91775), headless vs. interactive discrepancy (#97074) Exact reset times (#52894), catalog-price estimates for $0-reported providers (#59861), shared Go limits contradicting the docs (#60311)
Billing and plan flexibility A higher Team tier (#47509) Crypto payment for Go (#23153, closed)
Permissions and safety "Always allow" ignored in Cowork (#47180), actions beyond authorization (#60705) Silent external-directory writes (#54524), MCP OAuth token invalidation (#60612, fixed)
UI and ergonomics control Enter/Ctrl+Enter option (#89673), persistent Transcript view (#76577) Legacy sidebar (#48882), font size and line height (#54499)
Remote and multi-environment workflows Multi-repo remote sessions (#23627), GitLab (#12346) SSH crash (#64184), ACP/IDE streaming (#54371)
Platform stability Windows kernel leak (#96870), Wayland fd leak (#98725) Windows console flashing (#52266), Nix hash mismatches (#59882)

4. Differentiation Analysis

  • Business model. Claude Code's issues are about subscription tiers, 5-hour windows and Team seats. OpenCode's are about a free tier and a Go plan with shared limits and possibly misleading messages. Neither community trusts its metering.
  • Surface area. Claude Code is expanding across Desktop, Cowork scheduled tasks, cloud sessions, Chrome bridge and Remote Control, so its bugs involve a git proxy, permissions and OAuth. OpenCode is focused on the TUI/CLI and desktop, plus ACP/IDE integration and a native CLI port (#63477).
  • Technical direction. OpenCode's PRs show architectural work: shell as a Code Mode tool (#64256), experimental MCP Skills (#64157), a desktop browser pane (#63002), and a v2 plugin model. Claude Code's visible PR activity is a single Intune policy fix (#78049), which says little about its internal development. The digest likely understates vendor-side work that isn't done in public PRs.
  • Contribution model. OpenCode's community is shipping fixes (for example #64251 for the zombie processes). Claude Code's community mostly files issues and feature requests, and the digest notes a sweep that closed older issues, some as stale.
  • Target users. Claude Code serves subscription users, teams and enterprise (Intune/MDM, Team plan), including CI users. OpenCode serves model-agnostic users, including free-tier and Go-plan users and Nix, Android and SSH setups.

5. Community Momentum & Maturity

  • OpenCode looks like the faster-iterating project in this snapshot. It has many open PRs spanning bug fixes and features, and quick responses to its 2.3.0 regressions (a fix for the zombie leak was already in PR). The v2 migration is creating gaps, such as missing plugin APIs and a removed custom provider option.
  • Claude Code has the larger demand signal per issue, with 100–200+ 👍 on several items and a 304-comment closed thread. That is more engagement than the OpenCode threads, though the 378-comment free-tier megathread is the largest single item in either digest. Its issue lifecycle shows maintenance strain: several long-standing requests are closed as stale, and the /context verbosity complaint has been refiled at least four times. Treat the 304-comment thread (#60705) and the stale-closure sweep as signals about triage, not as proof of quality.
  • Both show a mature user base whose complaints concern operations (billing, quotas, permissions) rather than basic functionality.

6. Trend Signals

  1. Metering is now a product feature. Both communities want spend caps, accurate stats and predictable resets. Developers should check how a tool accounts for headless, CI and shared-limit use before committing to it. #97074 suggests headless mode costs more.
  2. Agent autonomy needs enforceable permissions. Complaints about ignored "Always allow" settings, silent writes outside the worktree, and directives treated as authorization show that safety defaults are still unreliable. Teams running unattended agents should audit permission behavior themselves.
  3. Remote, cloud and multi-repo work is the growth area, and also the least stable. Git proxy blocks, Remote Control failures, SSH crashes and ACP streaming gaps all fall here. Expect churn, and pin versions for production workflows.
  4. Extensibility and protocol work is converging. MCP (Skills, OAuth) and plugin APIs are central to OpenCode's roadmap. MCP OAuth refresh bugs affect real integrations.
  5. Practical guidance. For cost predictability and cloud features inside one vendor's ecosystem, Claude Code fits better, but weigh its open usage-accounting questions. For provider flexibility and open contribution, OpenCode fits better, but expect regressions around major version changes (2.3.0) and v2 migration.

Limits of this analysis: it rests on two community digests for one day, uses featured items rather than complete counts, and doesn't cover the other tools the wider project tracks.

Per-Tool Reports

Claude Code — anthropics/claude-code

Claude Code Skills Highlights

Source: anthropics/skills

Claude Code Skills Community Highlights (data as of 2026-11-17)

Data caveat: every PR's comment count came through as undefined, and all 👍 counts are 0. The PR ranking below is therefore based on the list order supplied, issue linkage and recent activity, not verified comment volume. Issue comment counts are intact. All 20 PRs shown are still open, and none are merged or draft.

1. Top Skills Ranking (PRs)

# PR What it does Highlights Status
1 #1742 mcp-builder fix Supports the mcp>=2 rename to streamable_http_client and the new custom-header mechanism. Fixes #1668. It is a compatibility break caused by an upstream SDK change. Last updated 2026-10-08. Open
2 #1298 skill-creator trigger evals Isolates trigger evals, fixes select() on Windows pipes, and stops runtime failures counting as non-triggers. It addresses the eval-accuracy bugs in issues #556 and #1352. Opened in June and still unmerged. Open
3 #1980 webapp-testing Removes shell=True from with_server.py (CWE-78 command injection). It is a security hardening change. Updated 2026-11-01. Open
4 #1792 docx accept_changes Reports a LibreOffice timeout as an error. It claims success only after confirming no revision marks remain. It removes a false-success path. Updated 2026-11-01. Open
5 #2019 xlsx recalc Resolves worksheet-scoped defined names and aliases in external_links_at_risk. Fixes #2013, which was false negatives on indirect external references. Open
6 #525 pyxel Adds a retro-game development skill. It covers headless runs, frame inspection and state checks. It is one of the longest-lived community skill submissions, from March, and was updated 2026-11-01. Open
7 #1245 notion-spec-to-implementation Turns product or tech specs into Notion tasks with acceptance criteria. It is bundled with a resume-auditor skill. It is workflow automation. Bundling two skills in one PR may slow review. Open
8 #1997 skill-creator YAML parsing Replaces hand-rolled frontmatter parsing with correct YAML scalar handling. Eval and optimization commands currently receive metadata that differs from SKILL.md. Open

2. Community Demand Trends (Issues)

  1. Reliable skill-creation and eval tooling. This is the strongest signal.
    • #556 (13 comments, 7 👍) reports a 0% trigger rate from claude -p.
    • #1352 reports parallel workers cross-matching skill UUIDs.
    • #202 asks for skill-creator best practices and token efficiency.
  2. Trust, provenance and security. #492 is the most-discussed item (46 comments). It concerns community skills distributed under the anthropic/ namespace and the resulting trust-boundary abuse. #412 proposed agent-governance patterns, and PR #1980 hardens shell execution.
  3. Context and token efficiency.
    • #1487: claude-api injects about 156k tokens in a single call.
    • #189: document-skills and example-skills install duplicate content.
    • #2064: descriptions need to say when to use a skill, not only what it does.
  4. Agent quality and memory skills. #1329 proposes compact-memory, and #1385 proposes a reasoning quality-gate pipeline (calibration, adversarial review, delivery verification).
  5. Sharing and distribution. #228 (17 comments, 8 👍) asks for org-wide skill sharing in Claude.ai.
  6. Document-skill robustness. #2018 (docx merge_runs.py writes invalid XML) and #1868 (slack-gif-creator gradient off by one) show active bug-hunting.
  7. Off-topic reports. #1143 (change account email, 18 👍, the highest in the set) and #62 (skills disappeared) are product or support issues. They are not skill requests.

3. High-Potential Pending Skills

These are small, well-scoped fixes tied to a filed issue, which are the likeliest to merge:

  • #1742 mcp-builder mcp>=2 fix. It is a breaking-SDK compatibility fix with a clear issue (#1668).
  • #1298 and #1997 fix the skill-creator evals, which have multiple open issues behind them.
  • #1980 removes a CWE-78 vulnerability.
  • #1792 and #2019 are narrow docx and xlsx correctness fixes.
  • #1950 is a docs update to the claude-api pause_turn guidance, tracking Python SDK 1.1.0.
  • #1975, #1976 and #1977 are one-line fixes, each linked to an issue (#1809, #1891, #1897).

Lower odds: net-new third-party skills (#1771 proofcore, #1703 md2video-audio, #1615 scnet-hpc, #514 document-typography). Several have sat since spring or summer with little maintainer response.

4. Skills Ecosystem Insight

The community's demand is concentrated on making the existing skills trustworthy and reliable: working skill-creator evals, secure scripts, correct document tooling and clear provenance. It is not asking for new domain skills.

Claude Code Community Digest: 2026-11-17

Today's Highlights

No new releases shipped in the last 24h. Activity centered on usage and cost: headless claude -p appears to burn the 5-hour window about 1.8× faster than interactive mode (#97074), and users are asking for a higher Team plan tier (#47509) and hard spend caps (#85422). Cowork and cloud sessions also had several reports of permission and git-push regressions. Many older issues were closed in a sweep, including several stale-labeled ones.

Releases

No new releases in the last 24h.

Hot Issues

  1. #97074: headless claude -p consumes ~1.8× more of the 5-hour window per token than interactive cli. It has a repro, 76 comments and 175 👍, the most upvoted bug in the batch. It matters for anyone running CI or automation on subscription plans. Users suspect an entrypoint-specific accounting difference.
  2. #47509: Team plan needs a Max 20x-equivalent tier. It has 75 comments and 201 👍. Premium seats (6.25× Pro) don't cover power users running agentic workflows, who currently buy individual Max 20x subscriptions instead.
  3. #76248: the Cloud/Cowork git proxy blocks all pushes outside the "authorized repository set". It has 42 comments. Since about July 10, even user-supplied fine-grained PATs fail, which breaks a previously working workflow. A CCR_TEST_GITPROXY rollout is suspected.
  4. #47180: Cowork scheduled tasks ignore "Always allow" permissions on macOS. It has 41 comments and 48 👍. Prompts reappear on every run, which defeats unattended scheduling.
  5. #12346: GitLab integration (repo connection, MRs, mobile access). It is nearly a year old, with 62 comments and 155 👍. It remains a persistent gap for non-GitHub teams.
  6. #89673: Desktop composer option for Enter = newline, Ctrl+Enter = submit. It has 117 👍. keybindings.json apparently doesn't cover the Desktop composer.
  7. #85422: token-burn circuit breaker with runtime-enforced spend caps. It asks for per-source attribution (hooks, plugins, subagents) and caps that stop runaway usage rather than just warn. It ties into the cost concerns above.
  8. #23627: multi-repository support for remote/web sessions. It has 90 👍 and complements the Cowork repo-authorization problem in #76248.
  9. #91775: the /usage Stats tab counts message.usage per transcript row instead of per message.id. Token totals are inflated roughly 2×. This undermines users' ability to audit their own consumption.
  10. #96870: Windows MSIX Desktop leaks kernel nonpaged pool. The leak happens when spawned processes open paths through an AppData junction, which is a bindflt.sys bug. It has a repro and could destabilize Windows machines over time.

Also notable:

  • #60705, now closed, had 304 comments. It reports /goal Stop-hook directives being treated as authorization for unrequested actions.
  • #66056 reports a right-click paste regression since about v2.1.167. Mouse reporting captures the click.

Key PR Progress

Only one PR was updated in this window, so I can't list 10:

  • #78049 (closed): fix(mdm) Set-ClaudeCodePolicy.ps1. The script built its destination from $env:ProgramFiles. Intune runs platform scripts in a 32-bit PowerShell host by default, so the policy was written to Program Files (x86). The PR fixes this, and the header only documented the 64-bit setting without enforcing it.

Feature Request Trends

  • Cost controls and visibility. Requests include hard spend caps (#85422), a higher Team tier (#47509), and accurate /usage stats (#91775). Analytics API coverage for subscription/OAuth users is also requested (#27780).
  • Cloud, remote and multi-repo workflows. These include multi-repo remote sessions (#23627), GitLab support (#12346), and portable project memory across machines (#25739).
  • Desktop and TUI ergonomics. Examples are configurable Enter/Ctrl+Enter behavior (#89673), persisting Transcript view mode (#76577), and a more compact /context (#64996).
  • Sandbox and platform capability. GPU passthrough in sandbox mode (#13108) is the main example.
  • Scheduling and automation. Timezone-aware cron for triggers (#50529) and a documented session JSONL schema (#53516) are both requested.

Developer Pain Points

  • Opaque usage accounting. Headless vs. interactive discrepancies (#97074), inflated /usage totals (#91775), and no way to cap runaway spend (#85422) leave users unable to trust or control consumption.
  • Cowork and cloud regressions. Git pushes are blocked (#76248), "Always allow" permissions are ignored (#47180), and Remote Control fails to re-attach with an HTTP 400 (#107503).
  • Windows and Desktop stability. There are kernel pool leaks (#96870), a Chrome bridge returning 403 "OAuth token forbidden" (#107922), and a Linux/Wayland renderer leaking /dev/shm file descriptors until the window freezes (#98725).
  • Model behavior trust. Users report acting beyond authorization and invented process consuming usage (#60705, #76987). A report of possible cross-session leakage (#74066) was also closed as stale.
  • Terminal regressions. Right-click paste broke after mouse reporting changes (#66056).
  • Recurring requests closed without resolution. The /context verbosity complaint has been filed at least four times (#64996).
OpenCode — anomalyco/opencode

OpenCode Community Digest — 2026-11-17

1. Today's Highlights

No new releases in the last 24h. Activity centers on 2.3.0 regressions (zombie processes under opencode-pty, TUI crash on SSH disconnect) and ongoing free-tier and Go-plan usage problems. Maintainers and contributors are also pushing a batch of fixes (ACP streaming, Bedrock content filter, shell scanning) and new work on Code Mode, MCP Skills and the desktop browser pane.

2. Releases

None in the last 24h.

3. Hot Issues

  1. #59387 Free tier issues megathread (378 comments, 👍28). It is the central place for "Free usage exceeded" errors and resets that never happen. It is the most-commented item by a wide margin and signals ongoing instability in the free tier.
  2. #48882 Restore the legacy UI with the persistent left sidebar (46 comments, 👍47). Users object to the sidebar redesign and want the classic two-panel layout back as an option.
  3. #23153 Pay Go with crypto (closed, 36 comments, 👍69). It has the most upvotes in the set. It shows demand for more payment options for the Go subscription.
  4. #50155 DeepSeek V4 Flash requires Global regions, but the Privacy setting is missing (26 comments). Paid Go users are blocked on this model because there is no way to select the region.
  5. #63817 pty: shell commands leave zombies under the opencode-pty daemon (2.3.0). This is a regression from 2.2.7. PRs #64251 and #64240 target it.
  6. #64184 TUI crashes with uncaught EIO on SSH disconnect (2.3.0). A graceful-shutdown failure that hits remote and SSH workflows.
  7. #60612 MCP: concurrent OAuth refreshes invalidate rotating refresh tokens (closed, severity:high). It broke credentials for Grafana Cloud and Buildkite MCP servers and has been fixed.
  8. #43250 keep.tokens not honoured in compaction (10 comments). Agent-driven sessions carry about 234K tokens against a 15K setting, which raises cost and context pressure.
  9. #54524 Built-in external_directory ask never prompts (👍9). A security-relevant permissions gap: writes outside the worktree succeed silently under default permissions.
  10. #60311 Go usage limits are shared across models, not per-model as documented (👍4). A docs and billing-expectation mismatch. It relates to #59861, where $0 cost reporting hides spend for Go sessions.

4. Key PR Progress

  1. #64251 Reap finished shell commands at exit. Fixes the 2.3.0 zombie leak in opencode-pty. It supersedes #64240.
  2. #64256 Make shell a Code Mode tool. Shell is no longer a top-level model tool and is called from scripts inside execute.
  3. #64157 Experimental MCP Skills support. Adds support for the MCP ext-skills spec.
  4. #63002 Signed-in desktop browser pane. Adds extensions, previews, prompts and agent safeguards. A companion security PR, #63614, which honors browser deny rules, was closed, as was #63611 on cookie encryption.
  5. #64262 Stream ACP turns woken by background shells. Related to the ACP slash-command output problem in #54371.
  6. #64260 Drop Bedrock tool calls when the content filter stops the reply. Prevents tools from running after content_filtered or guardrail_intervened.
  7. #64263 Keep unknown ANSI-C escapes per shell. Fixes the shell scanner rejecting valid $'...' strings.
  8. #64259 Case-insensitive session title search beyond ASCII. Fixes SQLite LIKE limits for non-ASCII titles.
  9. #61328 Restore doom-loop detection as an internal plugin for v2. Under design review.
  10. #63477 CLI: port to native. A large architectural effort, with a preview repo linked in the PR.

Also notable:

  • #64258 adds a typed i18n layer for the TUI. It was closed, as was the Chinese localization PR #64248.
  • #54499 adds font size and line height settings for desktop.

5. Feature Request Trends

  • Free and Go plan transparency: exact reset times (#52894), catalog-price estimates for $0-reported providers (#59861), crypto payments.
  • UI choice: a legacy sidebar layout (#48882), adjustable font size.
  • Plugin extensibility in v2: exposing the TUI composer to plugins (#51209).
  • TUI i18n: #37216, with two competing PRs closed.
  • Model features: display of Claude "progress update" thinking blocks (#55298); custom provider option missing (#59603).

6. Developer Pain Points

  • Free-tier and quota confusion: misleading limit messages, resets that never happen, and shared Go limits that contradict the docs. Subscription-sharing errors also appear on the ChatGPT side (#62529).
  • 2.3.0 regressions: zombie processes, SSH-disconnect crashes, and opencode upgrade via npm using --force and pulling about 2GB of optional dependencies (#63743).
  • v2 migration gaps: missing plugin APIs, the custom provider option gone, and compaction ignoring keep.tokens.
  • Platform issues: Windows console windows flashing about once per second (#52266), Nix hash mismatches (#59882), and Android incompatibility (#63791).
  • ACP and IDE integration: slash command output is not streamed (#54371).
  • Permissions and security surprises: silent external-directory writes and MCP OAuth token invalidation.

item.content:encoded:
MCP Ecosystem Digest 2026-11-17

Issues: 2 | PRs: 0 | Projects covered: 7 | Generated: 2026-11-16 16:42 UTC

  • MCP Servers
  • MCP Registry (official)
  • Awesome MCP Servers
  • Docker MCP Registry
  • Claude Plugins (official)
  • Awesome Claude Code
  • Awesome Agent Skills

MCP Deep Dive

MCP Servers Project Digest — 2026-11-17

1. Today's Overview

Activity on modelcontextprotocol/servers was very low in the last 24 hours: 2 issues were updated (both open), with no PRs updated and no new releases. Both issues come from the same author (Tanishq67m), they were filed on 2026-11-16, and both are tagged enhancement and v2. Both concern tool-description quality for small local models. The project looks quiet for the day, and no maintainer responses appear in the data (0 comments on both).

2. Releases

No new releases.

3. Project Progress

No PRs were merged or closed today, so no features or fixes advanced. Both open issues propose changes that no PR addresses yet.

4. Community Hot Topics

Neither issue has comments or reactions (0 comments, 0 👍 each), so there is no measurable community engagement yet. The two issues share a theme:

  • #5553: filesystem search_files description. The author measured on server-filesystem 2.0.0 and 2.2.0. They report that 2.3.0 ships the same description. They say that adding realistic examples to the description stops small models from refusing to search. It is a follow-up to #896 / #3419.
  • #5552: git git_log description. The author says the description doesn't state that results are newest-first, or that timestamp filters are optional. As a result, small models filter to an empty window. The author tested with the AgentGrade eval harness, MCP Python SDK 2.3.0, and qwen3:4b-instruct via Ollama at temperature 0.7.

Underlying need: Tool descriptions are the main interface for small and local models. Ambiguous or example-free descriptions cause measurable task failures. Users want descriptions that state default behavior, ordering, and optional parameters.

5. Bugs & Stability

No crashes or regressions were reported. The two issues describe behavioral failures that come from description quality rather than code defects, ranked by apparent impact:

  1. #5553: models refuse to use search_files, which makes the tool unusable for those models.
  2. #5552: the model gets empty git_log results from over-restrictive timestamp filters. This is a wrong-result failure.

No fix PRs exist for either issue.

6. Feature Requests & Roadmap Signals

Both issues are labeled v2 and enhancement, which suggests maintainers may consider them for v2-era work. Description edits are low-risk and small, so they could land quickly. The data shows no maintainer commitment, so any prediction is speculative. I would expect #5552, a one-line clarification, to be easier to accept than #5553, which adds examples to the description and may raise token-cost questions.

7. User Feedback Summary

  • Small models (e.g., qwen3:4b-instruct) are sensitive to the wording of tool descriptions.
  • Evaluation-harness users are measuring tool usability and reporting concrete failure rates (the full numbers are truncated in the data provided).
  • The feedback is constructive and evidence-based. It reflects use of the servers outside large frontier-model clients.

8. Backlog Watch

The provided data covers only the last 24 hours, so it doesn't show long-unanswered items. Two items need triage attention:

  • #5553: it references the older issues #896 and #3419, which suggests a recurring problem that has not been resolved.
  • #5552: it has no maintainer response yet.

Maintainers could review the older referenced issues to check for duplication or a shared fix.

Cross-Ecosystem Comparison

Cross-Project Comparison Report: MCP Ecosystem, 2026-11-17

Note: Awesome Claude Code had no activity. The data covers only the last 24h, and several lists show only the top 20 items, so conclusions are partial.

1. Ecosystem Overview

The projects in this set are not agent runtimes. They are the distribution and tooling layer of the MCP ecosystem: reference servers, registries, curated lists and plugin and skill catalogs. Activity is concentrated in intake, meaning submissions of new servers and skills. Review and triage are the bottleneck almost everywhere. Hosted and remote servers with streamable HTTP, OAuth and agent-trust concerns are gaining ground. Human-reported bugs in the first-party reference and plugin repos are slow to be resolved.

2. Activity Comparison

Health scores are my own qualitative judgment from the 24h data, not a measured metric.

Project Issues updated PRs updated Release Health (1–5) Note
MCP Servers (reference) 2 (open) 0 None 3 Quiet, no maintainer response visible
MCP Registry (official) 1 (open) 0 None 3 Quiet, one measurement report
Awesome MCP Servers 0 141 (132 open, 9 closed/merged) None 3 Very high intake, review throughput is the concern
Docker MCP Registry 0 50 (48 open, 2 closed/merged) None 2.5 Growing backlog, oldest PR is about a year old
Claude Plugins (official) 12 (all open) 4 (2 closed, 2 open bot bumps) None 3 Bug-heavy, with old high-demand items unresolved
Awesome Agent Skills 1 (closed) 50 (12 open, 38 closed/merged) None 4 Maintainers responsive, batch closes on Nov 15
Awesome Claude Code 0 0 None n/a No activity

No project shipped a release in the window.

3. MCP Servers's Position

Role. It is the reference implementation that other projects depend on. It is not a distribution channel.

Advantages vs peers

  • It is the canonical source of tool behavior, so its tool descriptions set expectations for the whole ecosystem.
  • Its issues are evidence-based. Both open issues (#5552, #5553) include eval results from a harness, a client SDK and a named small model.
  • Its v2 labels show a planned roadmap, which the curated lists lack.

Technical approach differences

  • Servers is code and tool-schema focused. The Registry deals with identity and namespace verification (#1860). Docker deals with packaging and catalog distribution. The lists and skill catalogs are content curation.

Community size

  • Servers is the smallest by 24h activity: 2 issues and 0 PRs, against 141 PRs for Awesome MCP Servers and 50 each for Docker and Agent Skills. Activity does not equal influence. Servers has low volume but high leverage, since each description change reaches every downstream user. Star and contributor counts are not in the data, so a true size comparison isn't possible.

Weak point. There are 0 comments and no maintainer response on either new issue.

4. Shared Technical Focus Areas

Need Projects Specifics
Tool and skill quality for small or local models MCP Servers Tool descriptions need examples, ordering and default behavior (#5552, #5553)
Verification and trust Registry, Awesome MCP Servers, Docker Endpoint ownership checks for 1,335 endpoints (#1860). Agent-output verification servers in the lists. Docker needs a policy for closed-source hosted servers
Remote and hosted endpoints Docker, Awesome MCP Servers, Registry Streamable HTTP, OAuth 2.1, no-auth endpoints, tools.json set to [] for dynamic discovery
Auth friction Claude Plugins, Docker GitHub plugin lacks dynamic client registration (#283, 82 👍). Docker PRs mention CIMD/DCR
Automated validation Awesome MCP Servers, Agent Skills, Docker Glama listing checks, link-rot validation (#1358, #1381), claude plugin validate
Review scalability Awesome MCP Servers, Docker, Agent Skills Large inflows with few closures
Scope and categorization Awesome MCP Servers, Agent Skills Category fragmentation, policy on multi-skill root entries, paid-service entries
Context fidelity in channel plugins Claude Plugins Telegram topics, quotes and Discord forwards (#1158, #929, #7133)

5. Differentiation Analysis

  • Reference code (MCP Servers). Target users are server authors and client developers. It is the source of tool behavior.
  • Identity layer (Registry). It targets publishers and clients that need provenance. Its design tension is between strict domain binding and inclusivity for GitHub-namespace and PaaS publishers.
  • Container catalog (Docker). It targets enterprise and Docker-based users. Its submissions are now mostly hosted servers rather than containers, which sits awkwardly with its container-based model.
  • Curated lists (Awesome MCP Servers, Awesome Agent Skills, Awesome Claude Code). Target discoverability, using PR-driven curation. Awesome Agent Skills covers instruction-based skills. Awesome MCP Servers covers executable servers. Agent Skills closed some MCP and browser-extension submissions as off-scope (#1414, #1395), which marks the boundary between the two types.
  • Plugin marketplace (Claude Plugins). It is vendor-run and pins plugin SHAs via bots. It has runtime bugs because it ships code, unlike the lists.

6. Community Momentum & Maturity

  • Tier 1, high intake: Awesome MCP Servers (141 PRs), Docker (50), Agent Skills (50). They are growing quickly. Agent Skills is keeping pace and the other two are building backlogs.
  • Tier 2, bug-driven maintenance: Claude Plugins (16 items). Bots keep pins current, but the Telegram and Discord issues have been open since March. The figma pin flow is churning, with three competing bump PRs.
  • Tier 3, low activity: MCP Servers, Registry, Awesome Claude Code. These are stable or quiet, and for the reference repos that mostly reflects a maturing spec. There was no release anywhere, so none is visibly rapidly iterating on a release basis.
  • Maturing: Registry policy is being revisited through measurement (#180 to #494 to #1860). Servers is moving toward v2.

7. Trend Signals

  1. Remote, hosted MCP is becoming the default submission type. Docker PRs dominantly describe hosted endpoints. Developers should plan for streamable HTTP and OAuth rather than stdio only.
  2. Tool descriptions are a measurable quality surface. Small-model evals show failures from ambiguous descriptions. State ordering, defaults and optional parameters, and include examples.
  3. Trust and verification are the open problem. Registry measurements, agent-output checkers and Glama or validate gates all point to it. Expect endpoint-ownership checks.
  4. Agent-assisted contributions are rising (🤖 disclosures in several lists). Curators will need automated gating.
  5. Payments and commercial skills are appearing (x402 USDC, paid-account skills). Maintainers lack a stance on gated entries.
  6. Remote-control channels need context fidelity. Threads, quotes, forwards and multi-instance handling matter for plugin builders.

Value for developers: Ship descriptions that work for small models. Support remote transports and OAuth. Publish verifiable identity metadata. Expect long review queues on third-party lists, and don't rely on them for timely distribution.

Peer Project Reports

MCP Registry (official) — modelcontextprotocol/registry

MCP Registry (Official) Project Digest — 2026-11-17

1. Today's Overview

Activity in modelcontextprotocol/registry was very low over the last 24 hours: one issue updated, no PRs updated, and no releases. The only activity is a new, open measurement report (#1860) about how well remote-endpoint domains match the namespaces they claim. There were no merges, closures, or bug reports. Nothing today signals a project-health problem. It looks like a quiet day, and the one item is a discussion-style proposal rather than a defect.

2. Releases

No new releases.

3. Project Progress

No PRs were merged or closed in the last 24 hours, so no features or fixes advanced today.

4. Community Hot Topics

There is only one active item, and it has 0 comments and 0 👍:

  • #1860 — Measurement: 95.07% of reverse-DNS endpoints sit on a domain their namespace implies; the other 1,335 have no runnable check (author: lanbass869-cell, opened 2026-11-16)
    • Context: According to the issue summary, #180 once required that a remote endpoint sit on the domain its server name claims. #494 removed that requirement in Nov 2025, because io.github.* publishers and PaaS users could not satisfy it. The replacement was meant to be self-identification by the endpoint.
    • Underlying need: The report gives a figure, 95.07% of reverse-DNS endpoints consistent with their namespace. It also counts 1,335 endpoints with no runnable verification. The need is a verifiable way to tie a registry entry to the party that controls the endpoint. The goal is to avoid the old domain-matching rule that excluded legitimate publishers.
    • Caveat: The digest only has the truncated summary. The proposed remedy and the exact measurement method are not visible here, so these figures are unverified.

5. Bugs & Stability

No bugs, crashes, or regressions were reported today. #1860 concerns trust and verification gaps, not a functional failure. No fix PRs are involved.

6. Feature Requests & Roadmap Signals

  • #1860 implicitly points toward a runnable endpoint-ownership check for the roughly 1,335 endpoints that currently have none. It most likely builds on the post-#494 self-identification design.
  • With no maintainer response, no linked PR, and no comments, a change in the next version is unlikely. A maintainer triage reply is the more realistic near-term outcome.

7. User Feedback Summary

There is no direct end-user feedback today. The author's measurement suggests that most entries (95.07%) are consistent, but a sizable minority cannot be checked automatically. The tension in the issue is between strict domain binding, which excludes GitHub-namespace and PaaS publishers, and loose verification, which leaves trust gaps.

8. Backlog Watch

The data covers only the last 24 hours, so no long-unanswered items can be identified from it. #1860 is new and uncommented, so it should get maintainer triage. Maintainers may also want to check how it relates to the earlier decisions in #180 and #494.

Awesome MCP Servers — punkpeye/awesome-mcp-servers

Awesome MCP Servers Digest, 2026-11-17

Source: punkpeye/awesome-mcp-servers

1. Today's Overview

Activity is high but is almost entirely new-server submissions. In the last 24h there were 141 PR updates (132 open, 9 merged/closed), no issue activity and no releases. The repo is a curated list, so the metric that matters is how fast submissions are reviewed. The numbering (PRs up to #19705) shows a steady inflow of new entries, and open PRs as old as #14718 (September) and #16055 (October) were touched today. Many submissions are marked 🤖🤖🤖, which suggests they were prepared with AI coding agents.

2. Releases

No new releases. The repository is a content list and does not publish versioned releases.

3. Project Progress

The data lists only a small subset of the 9 merged/closed PRs. Two closed PRs are visible, and neither is confirmed as a merge:

  • #18972: Rooster, a transcript-first Mac video editor with a local MCP server (Multimedia Process). It was closed on 2026-11-16 after being opened on 2026-11-09. The data does not say why.
  • #14718: Hyperconsciousness, a Rust knowledge store (Knowledge & Memory). It was closed after about two months open (created 2026-09-19).

Both carried the missing-glama label, so a missing Glama listing may be a factor. The data does not confirm that. The other 7 merged/closed PRs are not shown, so a merge count cannot be given.

4. Community Hot Topics

Comment counts are reported as undefined for every PR, so there is no comment or reaction signal (all 👍 are 0). The only usable signal is the submission pattern in the top PRs:

  • Developer Tools is the most crowded category: #19698 (trust-engine-mcp and signal-feed-mcp), #19695 (stackcheck-mcp), #19269 (cohors), #19633 (FailLoud, a done-check for agent output).
  • Finance and crypto: #19704 (CortexCloud, x402 USDC payments), #19696 (gammarips-harness), #19701 (bitcoindatalabs-mcp).
  • Browser, testing and QA: #19705 (Squally, Playwright run history), #19700 (agent-eyes).
  • Aggregators and remote or hosted servers: #19702 (Glyphcall, 650+ tools behind one endpoint), #19699 (Agent Flights).
  • Niche verticals: #19694 (Bible), #19693 (Project Zomboid), #19690 (ClipMind), #19703 (Zig H3 geospatial).

The underlying needs are:

  • Agent trust and verification. Several entries (FailLoud, trust-engine-mcp) target checking agent output.
  • Agent-native payments. CortexCloud uses x402.
  • Streamable HTTP hosted endpoints. More submissions offer these alongside stdio.

5. Bugs & Stability

No issues were reported and the data has no bug or regression signal. Reviewers do seem to run an automated validation check. PR titles carry labels such as has-emoji, valid-name, has-glama and missing-glama. Those labels were probably applied by a bot. Several PRs, for example #16055, #19700, #19699, #19695 and #19690, are tagged missing-glama. That is the most common blocker visible in the data.

6. Feature Requests & Roadmap Signals

There are no issues or explicit requests. Inferred signals from submissions:

  • Categories keep fragmenting, with entries for Gaming, Art & Culture, Travel and Marketing. A taxonomy review may be due.
  • Remote and hosted endpoints and official MCP Registry IDs are now commonly cited, for example in #19701 and #19698. The list may eventually need a field or tag for them.
  • Contributors increasingly disclose that an AI agent prepared the PR, as in #19700. This is an inference from the PR text.

7. User Feedback Summary

There is no direct feedback because there are no comments or issues. From the PR texts, contributors:

  • want listing in the right category and in alphabetical order.
  • cite Glama and the official MCP Registry as proof of quality.
  • stress safe, local, read-only or scoped access, as with Squally (read-only) and AdRails (plan → single-use plan ID → validate-before-write) in #17293.

8. Backlog Watch

Older open PRs that were updated today and may need maintainer attention:

  • #16055: Edworking MCP (Workplace & Productivity), open since 2026-10-09, flagged missing-glama.
  • #17293: AdRails (Marketing), open since 2026-10-22, flagged has-glama.
  • #19269: cohors (Developer Tools), open since 2026-11-12, flagged has-glama.

With 132 PRs open, review throughput is the main health concern. Only 9 PRs were closed or merged today against at least 3 PRs opened in the top-20 window alone. Note that the data shows only the top 20 of 141 PRs, so these figures are partial.

Docker MCP Registry — docker/mcp-registry

Docker MCP Registry Digest — 2026-11-17

Repo: docker/mcp-registry

1. Today's Overview

The registry shows a high volume of inbound submissions and no maintainer-side movement. In the last 24h, 50 PRs were updated (48 open, 2 merged/closed), while there were 0 issues and 0 releases. Nearly all of the 20 PRs shown are new "Add … remote MCP server" requests created on 2026-11-16, which suggests a submission wave for hosted servers. The visible data has no sign of review throughput: no comments are recorded on any listed PR. Activity is high on the intake side and low on the processing side.

2. Releases

No new releases.

3. Project Progress

Of the 50 updated PRs, only 2 were merged or closed. Neither appears in the top-20 list I was given, so I can't say which they were or what they changed. No feature or fix advancement can be attributed from this data. Every listed PR is still open.

4. Community Hot Topics

Comment counts are reported as undefined and 👍 reactions are 0 for every listed PR, so there is no real discussion signal. The ranking is therefore not meaningful. The themes visible in the submissions are:

  • Hosted/remote servers dominate. Most PRs describe closed-source or hosted endpoints with a streamable-http transport. Examples: #7226 (Clickflame and Supercanic), #7224 (Fiko, OAuth 2.1), #7222 (Agent Flights, no auth), #7221 (Weeklane).
  • Batch submissions. #7219 adds nine SportsDataHQ servers in one PR. #7226 and #5797 each add two.
  • Vertical and consumer domains. Examples: video (#7036 VideoDB, #7212 Dadan), app-store data (#7218), social/messaging (#7224, #7215), jobs (#7211), education (#7217).

The underlying need is that vendors want distribution through Docker's catalog for hosted services. They are not asking to containerize their code.

5. Bugs & Stability

No bugs, crashes or regressions were reported, since there are 0 issues. One signal to watch is that several PRs have no public source repo (for example #7225, #7221). That could conflict with the registry's open-source requirement, a question for maintainers rather than a bug.

6. Feature Requests & Roadmap Signals

No explicit feature requests exist. The submissions imply these signals:

  • Remote-server support is expected to keep growing as a first-class catalog type.
  • Several PRs use OAuth, with CIMD/DCR mentioned in #7224, and several use no auth. Clearer guidance on auth metadata may be needed.
  • "Dynamic" tool discovery with tools.json set to [] (#7224, #7222) may need schema or validation support.

These are my inferences. Nothing in the data states a roadmap.

7. User Feedback Summary

There is no direct user feedback, as no comments or issues were recorded. The PR templates show contributors following the "MCP Server Information" checklist. Authors stress read-only access, no-key access, and the multilingual or vertical value of their servers. No dissatisfaction was reported.

8. Backlog Watch

  • #744: "Add ebay-mcp local server", created 2025-11-20 and open about a year, so it is the oldest PR in the list. It was touched on 2026-11-16, which suggests the author is still waiting on review.
  • #5797: Levirge Brain and Search, open since 2026-10-17 (about 1 month) with no recorded comments.
  • #7036: VideoDB, open since 2026-11-13.
  • #7176: easyrender, open since 2026-11-15.

Health assessment: Contributor interest is strong, but 48 open PRs against 2 closed or merged in the window point to a growing review backlog. Maintainers may want to triage the new remote-server wave and the long-open PRs such as #744. Clarifying the policy for closed-source hosted servers would also help.

Caveat: the data shows only the top 20 of 50 PRs, and comment counts were unavailable. The conclusions above are limited accordingly.

Claude Plugins (official) — anthropics/claude-plugins-official

Claude Plugins (Official) Digest — 2026-11-17

1. Today's Overview

Activity is moderate and dominated by community issue reports rather than releases. Twelve issues and four PRs were updated in 24 hours, and no new releases shipped. All 12 issues are still open and none were closed. The PRs are almost all automated SHA bumps from bots. Issue traffic centers on the channel plugins (Telegram, Discord, fakechat). Maintainer response on those bug reports is not visible in the data.

2. Releases

No new releases.

3. Project Progress

Two PRs were closed. Neither is a feature or fix merge. Both are superseded figma pin bumps:

  • #7071, a claude[bot] bump of figma to 9d296d07 (v2.2.193), requested via Slack. Closed.
  • #6819, an automated figma bump to 7047cb45, opened 2026-10-20. Closed.

Two bot PRs remain open:

  • #7138, a figma bump to 5f3024c3.
  • #7137, a sap-ux-fiori-tools bump from 08afc41d to 0b3a88c4.

Both passed claude plugin validate. The figma plugin has had three competing bump PRs, and each one is closed or pending against the same old SHA, f2789420. That suggests the pin-update flow is churning rather than landing.

4. Community Hot Topics

  • #283, GitHub plugin auth failure (11 comments, 82 👍). By far the highest-demand item. It was opened in January 2026 and is still active. The GitHub MCP server at api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/ reports "does not support dynamic client registration". Users need a working official GitHub integration, and the fix likely requires a pre-registered OAuth client or a token-based config.
  • #1158, Telegram forum topics (7 comments). Users want message_thread_id support in supergroups.
  • #881, Telegram polling in non-channel instances (7 comments). The plugin steals updates from the intended instance.
  • #929, Telegram quoted replies dropped (4 comments, 9 👍). Claude cannot see the quoted message.
  • #6768, Discord allowlist rejection on Windows (5 comments).

The underlying need is that the channel plugins (Telegram, Discord) are used as real remote-control surfaces. Users want them to handle context correctly: threads, quotes, forwards, and multiple sessions.

5. Bugs & Stability

Ranked by severity. No linked fix PRs appear for any of them.

  1. #7136, security-guidance 2.0.20. The commit-review hook buffers the entire git show -p output before applying its file-count cut-off. On large commits this uses several GB of memory, a resource-exhaustion risk.
  2. #283, GitHub plugin auth failure. It blocks the plugin entirely and has been open for about 10 months.
  3. #881, Telegram polling in non-channel instances. Updates are stolen and messages are lost across multiple instances.
  4. Discord DM reply rejection, reported twice. #6768 is the Windows report. #7132 gives a likely root cause: the cached DMChannel.recipientId goes stale, and the issue suggests preferring dmChannelUsers.
  5. #7135, fakechat reply silently drops every file after the first.
  6. #7134, fakechat uploads can overwrite each other when two arrive in the same millisecond.
  7. #7133, Discord forwarded messages arrive empty because messageSnapshots is never read.

6. Feature Requests & Roadmap Signals

  • #1158, Telegram forum topics.
  • #929, Telegram reply-to content.
  • #1276, a separate admins role for permission relay. The author has already built a patch.
  • #7133, Discord forward support.

The Telegram requests from March are still unaddressed. The most likely near-term changes are the small, well-diagnosed Discord and fakechat fixes (#7132, #7134, #7135). Items that need design work are less likely soon: #1276 changes the permission model, and #1158 adds a new concept (thread-aware routing). Based on this data, I can't say how any of them will be prioritized.

7. User Feedback Summary

  • Users depend on channel plugins for remote sessions, and context loss is the main frustration. This covers quoted replies, forwards, and topics.
  • Permission relay is seen as too coarse. Everyone on allowFrom can approve tool use, which is a concern when the bot is shared.
  • Windows users hit Discord path and allowlist problems.
  • Authentication friction with the GitHub plugin affects many users, with 82 👍.
  • Several contributors (for example #7132 and #7135) submit detailed diagnoses with root causes. That signals engaged users, but it is also a reminder that the fixes are not landing quickly.
  • Not a user report: #7139 is a directory badge solicitation and can be treated as low-value.

8. Backlog Watch

  • #283, the GitHub plugin auth failure. It is about 10 months old with the highest engagement of any item. It needs a maintainer decision.
  • #881, the Telegram polling bug. It dates from March and has a clear root cause.
  • #1158, #929 and #1276, all Telegram requests open since March or April.
  • #6768 and #7132, duplicate Discord reports that should be triaged together.
  • The figma bump PRs (#7138 and earlier) need someone to merge one and stop the churn.

Health assessment: Bot automation keeps plugin pins current, but human-reported bugs, especially in the Telegram and Discord channel plugins, are slow to be resolved. A triage pass would help.

Awesome Claude Code — hesreallyhim/awesome-claude-code

No activity in the last 24 hours.

Awesome Agent Skills — VoltAgent/awesome-agent-skills

Awesome Agent Skills Digest, 2026-11-17

1. Today's Overview

VoltAgent/awesome-agent-skills is a curated list that takes community submissions through PRs. It had 50 PRs and 1 issue updated in the last 24 hours, and no releases. Of the PRs, 12 are open and 38 are closed or merged. A wave of new skill submissions arrived on Nov 15–16 (#1415–#1426), and a maintainer pass on Nov 15 closed a batch of older PRs. Activity is high and almost all of it is submissions. Review capacity looks like the bottleneck, and the 12 open PRs are all fresh (no comments).

2. Releases

No new releases.

3. Project Progress

The data doesn't separate merged PRs from closed-unmerged ones, so I can't say which of these actually landed. The closed items, all updated Nov 15, fall into three groups.

  • Cleanup of retired listings.
    • #1358 removes the obsolete OpenAI frontend-skill and develop-web-game listings and closes issue #1351.
    • #1381 fixes Notion source links that pointed to a removed directory, and moves a misplaced community entry.
  • Skill submissions closed.
    • Marketing and SEO: #1334 (akii schema-markup), #1365 (everyinfra/seo-skills).
    • Specialized Domains: #1366 (everyinfra-agent-plugins).
    • Productivity: #1405 (generate-qr).
  • Off-scope submissions closed. #1414 (an MCP server) and #1395 (a Chrome extension, "Claude to PDF") are not skills. They were probably closed for that reason, though the data doesn't say.

4. Community Hot Topics

No item has any comments or reactions. The comment counts show as undefined and the 👍 count is 0 everywhere. The themes are below.

  • Marketing and SEO skills dominate. #1423 (gomarble, 60 skills), #1422 (RedYA Xiaohongshu), #1420 (ghostfeed), #1418 (leadsets, 50 skills) and #1416 (harborrank, 18 skills). Vendors want visibility in the list, and many of their skills need paid accounts or API keys.
  • Development and testing. #1425 (scandiary, an accessibility audit with axe-core) and #1419 (hyper-elements).
  • Resubmission after feedback. #1426 (suprsend) resubmits #1360 as a single root-repo entry, as a maintainer suggested. This shows that contributors act on review guidance.
  • Other submissions. #1417 (contextcore, context engineering), #1424 (modellix-design), #1421 (inbox-envoy), #1415 (grill-me-visually).

5. Bugs & Stability

There are no crashes or regressions, since this is a content repository. One data-quality bug was reported and has been fixed.

  • #1351 (closed): officialskills.sh listed the removed OpenAI frontend-skill with a broken install path. The fix is #1358, which also removes develop-web-game.
  • #1381 shows that link rot against upstream sources is a recurring problem. Entries drift when upstream directories are removed.

6. Feature Requests & Roadmap Signals

There are no explicit feature requests. The signals below are inferences from the submissions.

  • Submitters say there is no "AI and Data" subcategory (#1366). A new category, or a better home for data and platform skills, may follow.
  • Marketing is heavily oversubscribed. A split into SEO, ads and GTM subcategories is plausible.
  • Large multi-skill repos (gomarble, leadsets, ghostfeed) suggest a policy on one root entry versus per-skill entries, as in #1426.
  • Contributors want automated link validation, because of the retired-listing cleanup.

7. User Feedback Summary

  • Contributors mainly want discoverability and credibility. Submissions cite stars (100+), licenses (MIT) and public availability.
  • Many skills are commercial or gated behind a paid account or API key (Ghostfeed, Modellix, RedYA). Maintainers may need a stance on these.
  • Contributors are disclosing authorship ("I maintain this") and AI assistance (the 🤖 note in #1365).
  • Downstream consumers, such as officialskills.sh users, are affected when listings go stale.

8. Backlog Watch

  • All 12 open PRs, #1415 through #1426, are under 3 days old. They have no comments or maintainer responses yet.
  • Maintainer attention is needed on the large multi-skill submissions (#1423, #1418, #1420). They need a decision on scope and on paid-service skills.
  • No old, important open issues appear in this window. Older backlog items outside the 24h window can't be assessed from this data.

Health assessment: Submission volume is very high and maintainers are responsive (a batch of closes on Nov 15). The main risks are review throughput and curation quality, because many entries are promotional or gated.
